screens.title: AWS Global Infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by building a mental model of AWS’s global footprint so you can design resilient, fast applications. AWS separates its infrastructure into Regions, which are independent geographic areas, and Availability Zones, which are physically separate data center locations inside a Region. Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches sit even closer to users to cache and serve content with minimal delay. Understanding these layers helps you make practical choices: which Region to host data in for legal compliance, how many Availability Zones to use for fault tolerance, and when to leverage CloudFront for content delivery. For example, placing user profiles for European customers in a Europe-based Region reduces legal risk and improves latency, while distributing web servers across two or more AZs prevents a single data center failure from taking your site offline. A common trap is to pick a single AZ because it seems cheaper; that creates a single point of failure. As we walk through this lesson, you’ll see clear design patterns, concrete trade-offs, and short steps you can apply immediately when selecting Regions, designing across AZs, and using Edge Locations. Think about a recent outage you heard about: how would a multi-AZ design have changed the outcome?

screens.title: What is an AWS Region?
screens.narratorSegment: An AWS Region is a geographic area that contains multiple data centers clustered together by AWS. Regions are intentionally isolated from each other to provide fault boundaries: a problem in one Region should not affect other Regions. This isolation supports legal and compliance requirements where data must remain in a particular country or jurisdiction. For example, you might choose eu-west-1 for Irish jurisdiction or eu-central-1 for Germany-based residency. Regions also let you place resources near your users to reduce network latency. When you launch services, you must choose the Region that will host your data and compute, and that decision has practical consequences: service availability varies by Region, and pricing can differ slightly. A common misconception is that a Region is a single data center; in reality it is a collection of Availability Zones and many physical data centers. A good rule of thumb is to pick Regions for proximity, legal compliance, and required service availability. Takeaway: think region-first for residency and latency goals, and always confirm service availability and pricing in your chosen Region before you design a deployment.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is an AWS Region?
Definition

A Region is a physical geographic area that contains AWS infrastructure and serves as an isolated unit for resilience and compliance.

Why choose a Region
  • Data residency and legal compliance.
  • Lower latency by placing resources near users.
  • Service availability and cost considerations.
Concrete example

If most customers are in Europe, use eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 to keep user data in-region and reduce access time.

Key takeaway

Regions set the scope for where resources live; choose them based on compliance and latency first.

Common misconceptions
  • Thinking a Region is one data center. It contains multiple AZs and data centers.
  • Assuming all services are available in every Region. Service availability varies.
Scenario card
Selecting a Region for EU privacy

Requirement: user profiles for EU residents must be stored in the EU. Action: choose a European Region such as eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 to meet residency rules.

screens.title: Choosing a Region: trade-offs and criteria
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a Region involves trade-offs. The primary criteria are latency (how close your users are), data residency (laws that require data to remain in certain locations), available services (not every feature exists in every Region), and cost differences. Start by prioritizing legal and compliance requirements: if laws force data to remain in a jurisdiction, that requirement overrides latency. If compliance is flexible, choose the Region closest to the largest portion of your users to reduce round-trip time. Next, verify that the services you need are offered in the chosen Region; some specialized services roll out gradually. Cost is usually a secondary factor but can influence choice for large-scale deployments. A common mistake is optimizing only for cost or proximity and forgetting compliance or service availability. For example, picking a cheaper Region that lacks a required managed database service will create operational debt. Practice: list your priorities for a given app — compliance first, then latency, then services, then cost — and check each Region against that list. Takeaway: document your selection rationale so future teams understand why a Region was chosen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Choosing a Region
Decision factors
Latency

Place resources close to users to reduce response time and improve experience.

Data residency

Legal or regulatory requirements that mandate where data may be stored.

Service availability

Confirm that the services and instance types you need exist in the Region.

Cost

Pricing varies slightly — include cost in your total cost of ownership analysis.

Quick checklist
  1. Confirm compliance and data residency needs for the workload.
  2. Choose the nearest Region to the largest user base when legal constraints allow.
  3. Verify required services and instance families exist in the Region.
  4. Estimate costs and operational impact; document the choice rationale.
Scenario card
Example decision

North American app: choose us-east-1 or us-west-2 for proximity. If a managed service you need exists only in us-east-1, select that and document why.

screens.title: What is an Availability Zone (AZ)?
screens.narratorSegment: An Availability Zone, or AZ, is one or more discrete data centers within a Region that are engineered to be isolated from failures in other AZs. Each AZ has independent power, networking, and connectivity, and they are connected to other AZs in the Region with high-bandwidth, low-latency links. This construction allows you to design systems that remain available even when one AZ has a hardware failure or outage. For example, running web servers in us-east-1a and us-east-1b and placing your database replica in the second AZ gives you redundancy: if one AZ loses power, the other continues serving traffic. A common misconception is that spreading instances across AZs automatically makes your application fully resilient; you must also architect for replication, load balancing, and state management. Best practice is to distribute stateless tiers across multiple AZs and replicate stateful data stores or use managed services that offer multi-AZ redundancy. Takeaway: treat AZs as independent failure domains within the same Region and design replication and failover accordingly. What is an Availability Zone (AZ)? means use multiple azs to prevent single data center failures from causing downtime; plan replication and failover intentionally.. In practical terms, azs are isolated data centers within a region that provide fault isolation and high availability.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Availability Zone
Definition & properties
  • AZs are isolated physical locations inside a Region with independent power and networking.
  • AZs are interconnected with low-latency fiber to enable synchronous replication and failover.
  • Design across AZs for high availability and disaster tolerance.
Concrete example

Run application servers across us-east-1a and us-east-1b and place database replicas so that an AZ outage still leaves a healthy replica operational.

Design guidance
Stateless tiers

Distribute across AZs behind a load balancer for horizontal availability.

Stateful tiers

Use replication or managed multi-AZ services to keep data available if an AZ fails.

Key takeaway

Distribute components and plan replication; AZs are the primary local fault domains.

screens.title: Designing for multi-AZ high availability
screens.narratorSegment: Designing high availability within a Region follows repeatable steps you can apply to nearly any application. Start by identifying stateless and stateful tiers. Stateless tiers, like web front ends, can scale horizontally and should be placed across multiple AZs behind a load balancer. Statefulness, such as user profiles or transaction records, requires replication: use database replicas or managed multi-AZ services to keep data durable. Next, deploy redundant instances of critical services across at least two AZs and configure health checks and automatic failover so traffic moves to healthy endpoints when an AZ is impacted. Third, practice failure scenarios and automation: test AZ failover using simulated outages and ensure startup scripts, configuration management, and infrastructure-as-code tools can rebuild capacity in another AZ. Also plan for cross-AZ networking — ensure subnets, routing, and security groups permit multi-AZ communication. A common mistake is assuming replication is instantaneous; design for eventual consistency where required and verify recovery time objectives. Example: host app servers in AZ A and B, database in AZ A with a synchronous replica in AZ B, and use automated DNS health checks to fail over. Takeaway: follow the identify-distribute-replicate-test cycle to achieve predictable availability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Designing for multi-AZ
Step-by-step
  1. Identify stateless and stateful tiers and their resilience needs.
  2. Deploy stateless tiers across at least two AZs behind a load balancer.
  3. Replicate stateful data or use multi-AZ managed services.
  4. Automate failover and recovery; practice real failover tests.
Example deployment

Web servers in AZ A and B; primary database in AZ A with a synchronous replica in AZ B; load balancer routes traffic and health checks steer traffic to healthy AZs.

Supporting cards
Key takeaway

Automate and test failover; distribution alone is not sufficient without replication and health checks.

Common-mistake

Keeping all state in a single AZ because it’s slightly cheaper adds a single point of failure.

Pro tip

Use managed multi-AZ database offerings when possible to simplify replication and failover.

screens.title: Edge Locations and CloudFront
screens.narratorSegment: Edge Locations are points of presence located in major cities and population centers that cache content for faster delivery to end-users. Amazon CloudFront uses these Edge Locations to store copies of static and dynamic assets like images, videos, and web pages so requests can be served close to the user rather than traveling back to the origin Region. This dramatically cuts latency for users who are far from your origin. For instance, a user in Sydney requesting content hosted in us-east-1 will get a faster response if CloudFront serves the content from a Sydney Edge Location. Edge Locations are designed for low-latency delivery but are not a substitute for regional data storage for legal reasons. If content isn’t found at an Edge Location, CloudFront queries a Regional Edge Cache or the origin Region. Misconception to avoid: caching speeds read access but does not change where authoritative data is stored. Takeaway: use Edge Locations when you need to reduce latency for content delivery, and plan what to cache carefully to respect data residency and freshness requirements. Edge Locations and CloudFront means edge locations reduce latency by caching content near users; they complement regions and azs but do not change origin data residency.. In practical terms, edge locations cache content to serve users with minimal latency using cloudfront.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Edge Locations
What Edge Locations do

Cache copies of frequently requested content to reduce latency and offload origin servers.

Use cases
  • Delivering images, videos, and static website assets globally.
  • Reducing origin load and bandwidth costs for popular assets.
Behavior

If an Edge Location lacks an item, it checks a Regional Edge Cache, then the origin, minimizing repeated long trips to the Region.

Concrete example

A video stored in us-east-1 is delivered to an Australian user through an Edge Location in Sydney, reducing buffering and improving start time.

Misconception

Edge caching does not change where the authoritative copy of data resides; it improves delivery speed for cached assets only.

screens.title: Regional Edge Caches — the second tier
screens.narratorSegment: Regional Edge Caches act as an intermediate caching layer between Edge Locations and your origin Region. They hold a larger set of content than individual Edge Locations, which means that if an Edge Location misses a request, the Regional Edge Cache often can serve it without contacting the origin. This reduces load on your primary application servers and shortens fetch paths for content that is less frequently accessed but still beneficial to cache. Think of Edge Locations as neighborhood bookdrops and Regional Edge Caches as a regional library that holds more titles. When content is requested, CloudFront looks at the nearest Edge Location, then the Regional Edge Cache, then the origin. Use Regional Edge Caches when you serve a global audience with a mix of very popular and moderately popular assets — they balance storage and reach. A misconception is believing regional caches replace the need for origin capacity planning; they reduce origin load but do not eliminate the need to size and protect origin infrastructure. Takeaway: add Regional Edge Caches for layered caching that reduces origin traffic and improves global cache hit rates.

keyIdea.text: Use Regional Edge Caches as a larger cache tier to improve hit rates and reduce origin load before resorting to the origin Region.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Regional Edge Caches
Role and behavior

Regional Edge Caches are larger caching locations positioned between Edge Locations and the origin. They store more content and reduce the number of requests that reach your origin Region.

Flow

Client → Edge Location → Regional Edge Cache → Origin Region.

When to use

Global distribution of moderate-popularity assets benefits from Regional Edge Caches to increase hit ratio.

Analogy

Edge Locations are neighborhood caches; Regional Edge Caches are regional libraries that keep a wider selection, reducing trips to the origin library.

Misconception

Regional Edge Caches reduce origin hits but do not replace the need for resilient and scalable origin servers.

screens.title: Deployment best practices across the global infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: When you design for the AWS global infrastructure, combine the strengths of Regions, AZs, and Edge caching into a holistic pattern. Start with region choice for compliance and proximity. Within that Region, place critical components across at least two AZs: stateless compute in multiple AZs behind load balancers, and stateful data replicated or managed multi-AZ. Use CloudFront Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches for static and cacheable assets to accelerate global delivery while keeping the authoritative data in the chosen Region for compliance. Also design for automated recovery: use infrastructure-as-code, health checks, and auto-scaling so capacity is replaced quickly after failures. Consider cross-Region replication for disaster recovery, where necessary, to recover from a Region-level failure. A pitfall is over-distributing state without clear consistency plans — cross-AZ replication is strong, but cross-Region replication often involves different replication and recovery considerations. Example pattern: primary Region hosts live data and services across AZs; cross-Region snapshots or asynchronous replication provide disaster recovery; CloudFront caches deliver assets worldwide. Takeaway: a layered architecture uses Region, AZ, and Edge tiers together with automation and replication strategies to meet availability, latency, and compliance goals.

screens.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Recognizing common mistakes helps you avoid fragile designs. One frequent error is deploying all resources in a single Availability Zone to save a small amount of cost; this creates a single point of failure and risks prolonged downtime if that AZ fails. Another is ignoring data residency; storing sensitive user data outside required jurisdictions can cause legal and compliance problems. A third mistake is over-relying on Edge Locations as a security or residence solution — Edge caching speeds delivery but does not change the authoritative storage location of your data. Some teams assume cross-Region distribution is always better; cross-Region replication increases complexity and latency for writes, so use it when Region-level disaster recovery is required. Finally, a planning misstep is neglecting to test failover and recovery procedures. Practice routine simulated failures and automation to ensure recovery goals are met. Example contrast: single-AZ cheap option might save money short term but can lead to expensive outages later. Takeaway: design choices should be documented and tested; avoid shortcuts that compromise availability or compliance. screens.title: Hands-on scenario: global gaming platform
screens.narratorSegment: Let's apply what you've learned to a concrete scenario: a gaming platform with most users in North America and planned expansion to Europe and Asia. First, choose a primary Region for North America — us-east-1 is often chosen because it is centrally located for large North American audiences and offers broad service availability. Next, ensure high availability within that Region by placing web servers across at least two AZs and replicating your user database across those AZs. For Europe, to meet data residency for user profiles, select a European Region such as eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 and store EU user profile data there while using cross-Region replication or synchronization for non-sensitive global data if needed. For low-latency delivery of game assets worldwide, configure Amazon CloudFront with Edge Locations and enable Regional Edge Caches to reduce origin hits. A common misconception is that copying all data globally avoids residency issues — it does not. Instead, ensure personal data stays in the European Region while caching public assets at the Edge. Takeaway: combine Region choice for residency, multi-AZ for resilience, and CloudFront for performance to meet this gaming platform’s needs.

screens.title: Data center and physical infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: At the lowest level of AWS’s hierarchy are the data centers — physical facilities that house racks of servers, networking, and power systems. A single Availability Zone can contain one or more data centers, each designed with redundant power and connectivity. These physical data centers are purpose-built to reduce risk from localized failures and to enable the high-bandwidth links between AZs that support replication and failover. When you design systems, remember that underlying physical separation matters: AZs are separated by meaningful distances within a Region to avoid common environmental risks but are close enough to support low-latency communication. A misconception is to assume that AZ names like us-east-1a or us-east-1b correspond to identical physical characteristics across different accounts — AZ identifiers may map differently per account, so design for AZ independence without relying on specific lettered names. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three compact concepts to remember. First, a Region is a top-level geographic boundary for infrastructure: choose it for legal, latency, and service availability reasons. Second, Availability Zones are isolated failure domains within a Region that you should use to distribute compute and replicate data so your systems continue operating if one AZ has problems. Third, Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches are caching layers used by CloudFront to deliver content quickly to users; they improve performance but do not change where authoritative data is stored. Keep these three ideas in mind when mapping an application to AWS: Region for residency, AZs for local resilience, and Edge caching for global performance. A final practical tip is to document why you chose a Region and to test AZ failover regularly so your design choices remain valid over time.

fullNarratorScript:
We begin by building a mental model of AWS’s global footprint so you can design resilient, fast applications. AWS separates its infrastructure into Regions, which are independent geographic areas, and Availability Zones, which are physically separate data center locations inside a Region. Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches sit even closer to users to cache and serve content with minimal delay. Understanding these layers helps you make practical choices: which Region to host data in for legal compliance, how many Availability Zones to use for fault tolerance, and when to leverage CloudFront for content delivery. For example, placing user profiles for European customers in a Europe-based Region reduces legal risk and improves latency, while distributing web servers across two or more AZs prevents a single data center failure from taking your site offline. A common trap is to pick a single AZ because it seems cheaper; that creates a single point of failure. As we walk through this lesson, you’ll see clear design patterns, concrete trade-offs, and short steps you can apply immediately when selecting Regions, designing across AZs, and using Edge Locations. Think about a recent outage you heard about: how would a multi-AZ design have changed the outcome?

In this section you will develop four practical skills that let you design for resilience and performance on AWS. First, you will be able to describe the hierarchical structure of AWS infrastructure — what Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations are — and why that hierarchy matters for reliability. For example, you will explain how an outage in one Region does not affect another. Second, you will understand why Regions exist: to provide geographical isolation, meet data residency requirements, and place resources near users to reduce latency. A concrete use case is storing European user profiles in a European Region to meet compliance. Third, you will explain the role of Availability Zones: how running resources in multiple AZs increases fault tolerance and supports automated failover. You’ll practice an AZ deployment pattern for web servers and databases. Fourth, you will learn how Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches speed content delivery through CloudFront and when to use them. You will also identify best practices for deploying across Regions and AZs to maximize resilience and performance. Each objective is a practical milestone you can verify by mapping a hypothetical application to Regions, AZs, and Edge caches.

Beyond definitions, you will practice decision-making with scenarios that mirror real requirements. You will evaluate Region choices for latency and data residency, sketch multi-AZ deployments to ensure failover, and select where to place caches for media delivery. Each objective is paired with a verified milestone: labeling maps, designing AZ-redundant architectures, and recommending CloudFront for content. For example, in a practice task you will choose us-east-1 for a North American user base and then propose AZ placement for web and database tiers. You will also identify a European Region to store user profiles for compliance. These exercises force you to balance trade-offs: latency versus jurisdiction, cost versus resilience. Common misconceptions are covered: for instance, Edge Locations speed content but do not replace regional data storage for compliance. At the end you will have clear, testable answers and design sketches that demonstrate competency rather than memorization.

An AWS Region is a geographic area that contains multiple data centers clustered together by AWS. Regions are intentionally isolated from each other to provide fault boundaries: a problem in one Region should not affect other Regions. This isolation supports legal and compliance requirements where data must remain in a particular country or jurisdiction. For example, you might choose eu-west-1 for Irish jurisdiction or eu-central-1 for Germany-based residency. Regions also let you place resources near your users to reduce network latency. When you launch services, you must choose the Region that will host your data and compute, and that decision has practical consequences: service availability varies by Region, and pricing can differ slightly. A common misconception is that a Region is a single data center; in reality it is a collection of Availability Zones and many physical data centers. A good rule of thumb is to pick Regions for proximity, legal compliance, and required service availability. Takeaway: think region-first for residency and latency goals, and always confirm service availability and pricing in your chosen Region before you design a deployment.

Choosing a Region involves trade-offs. The primary criteria are latency (how close your users are), data residency (laws that require data to remain in certain locations), available services (not every feature exists in every Region), and cost differences. Start by prioritizing legal and compliance requirements: if laws force data to remain in a jurisdiction, that requirement overrides latency. If compliance is flexible, choose the Region closest to the largest portion of your users to reduce round-trip time. Next, verify that the services you need are offered in the chosen Region; some specialized services roll out gradually. Cost is usually a secondary factor but can influence choice for large-scale deployments. A common mistake is optimizing only for cost or proximity and forgetting compliance or service availability. For example, picking a cheaper Region that lacks a required managed database service will create operational debt. Practice: list your priorities for a given app — compliance first, then latency, then services, then cost — and check each Region against that list. Takeaway: document your selection rationale so future teams understand why a Region was chosen.

An Availability Zone, or AZ, is one or more discrete data centers within a Region that are engineered to be isolated from failures in other AZs. Each AZ has independent power, networking, and connectivity, and they are connected to other AZs in the Region with high-bandwidth, low-latency links. This construction allows you to design systems that remain available even when one AZ has a hardware failure or outage. For example, running web servers in us-east-1a and us-east-1b and placing your database replica in the second AZ gives you redundancy: if one AZ loses power, the other continues serving traffic. A common misconception is that spreading instances across AZs automatically makes your application fully resilient; you must also architect for replication, load balancing, and state management. Best practice is to distribute stateless tiers across multiple AZs and replicate stateful data stores or use managed services that offer multi-AZ redundancy. Takeaway: treat AZs as independent failure domains within the same Region and design replication and failover accordingly. In practical terms, azs are isolated data centers within a region that provide fault isolation and high availability.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing high availability within a Region follows repeatable steps you can apply to nearly any application. Start by identifying stateless and stateful tiers. Stateless tiers, like web front ends, can scale horizontally and should be placed across multiple AZs behind a load balancer. Statefulness, such as user profiles or transaction records, requires replication: use database replicas or managed multi-AZ services to keep data durable. Next, deploy redundant instances of critical services across at least two AZs and configure health checks and automatic failover so traffic moves to healthy endpoints when an AZ is impacted. Third, practice failure scenarios and automation: test AZ failover using simulated outages and ensure startup scripts, configuration management, and infrastructure-as-code tools can rebuild capacity in another AZ. Also plan for cross-AZ networking — ensure subnets, routing, and security groups permit multi-AZ communication. A common mistake is assuming replication is instantaneous; design for eventual consistency where required and verify recovery time objectives. Example: host app servers in AZ A and B, database in AZ A with a synchronous replica in AZ B, and use automated DNS health checks to fail over. Takeaway: follow the identify-distribute-replicate-test cycle to achieve predictable availability.

Edge Locations are points of presence located in major cities and population centers that cache content for faster delivery to end-users. Amazon CloudFront uses these Edge Locations to store copies of static and dynamic assets like images, videos, and web pages so requests can be served close to the user rather than traveling back to the origin Region. This dramatically cuts latency for users who are far from your origin. For instance, a user in Sydney requesting content hosted in us-east-1 will get a faster response if CloudFront serves the content from a Sydney Edge Location. Edge Locations are designed for low-latency delivery but are not a substitute for regional data storage for legal reasons. If content isn’t found at an Edge Location, CloudFront queries a Regional Edge Cache or the origin Region. Misconception to avoid: caching speeds read access but does not change where authoritative data is stored. Takeaway: use Edge Locations when you need to reduce latency for content delivery, and plan what to cache carefully to respect data residency and freshness requirements. Regional Edge Caches act as an intermediate caching layer between Edge Locations and your origin Region. They hold a larger set of content than individual Edge Locations, which means that if an Edge Location misses a request, the Regional Edge Cache often can serve it without contacting the origin. This reduces load on your primary application servers and shortens fetch paths for content that is less frequently accessed but still beneficial to cache. When content is requested, CloudFront looks at the nearest Edge Location, then the Regional Edge Cache, then the origin. Third, High Availability and Fault Tolerance: high availability is the goal of keeping services operational for most of the time, while fault tolerance is the system’s ability to continue operating when components fail. Use these terms when documenting architectural decisions and when planning failover tests. Closing reflection: which of these terms most affects your current project and what immediate action will you take to align architecture with it?
